title: I’m feeling more optimistic about American politics
author: Noah Smith
text:
I’m feeling more optimistic about American politicsAnd it’s not *just* because I prefer the Democrats.Noah SmithNov 14, 2026∙ PaidPhoto by Abdullah Konte on Unsplash“Partisanship is a helluva drug,” as they say. When your preferred party is in power, the sun seems to shine a little brighter, the birds sing a little more sweetly, and there’s a spring in your step as you walk past the homeless encampments and sterile single-family-home-only neighborhoods of your American city. Foreigners from countries where politics is less contentious, like Japan, will never know this joy. Anyway, this natural partisan sentiment makes it very hard for me to write about developments in American politics. I would like to give you some analysis that’s more informative than “Yay, Democrats won an election!”. I do consider myself a Democrat, after all (even though I’m registered as an Independent). There has never been a point in my entire life when I’d have told you that the Republican presidential candidate was a better pick than the Democrat (though 2012 was fairly close). I regularly bemoan the state of the Democratic Party, but somehow the Republicans always find some way to be Even Worse.This has been the unfortunate reality for most people in America for years now. Disgust and dissatisfaction with both parties have grown, as both have become more extremist. But there was little they could do except keep voting for the lesser of two evils, while tuning out political news and expressing anger at the whole system. It got so bad that in my New Year’s essay, I even entertained the notion that liberal democracy itself had suffered a generational failure:Where does a liberal go from here?Noah Smith·Jan 4Read full storyTo be honest, I still entertain that notion. Reading that essay again, there’s not much I would change. But on the margin, recent events have made me feel more optimistic about where American politics is going. A lot of this is downstream of the midterm elections. Trump has turned the Republican Party into something truly awful, and it’s refreshing to see America punish the GOP for going along with that transformation:Croaky Caiman | The Rational Purview@RationalPurviewMAGA inherited a Republican Party with 54 senators, 247 House seats, and 31 governors.

They coopted the tea party that led to these wins and ran on pure populism with no actual guiding conservative principles other than whatever one guy said at any given moment and what his…Stinson Norwood @snorman1776Maybe true maga has never really been tried?3:51 PM · Nov 12, 2026 · 262K Views31 Replies · 163 Reposts · 800 LikesBut my optimism isn’t just about the fact that Democrats won — it’s also about how they won, and what they seem likely to do with their victory. Here I’ve been pleasantly surprised so far. And there are also some scattered signs that our leaders are starting to take our substantive policy challenges more seriously, instead of just relying on partisanship and culture wars. Basically, I see three broad positive trends:The Democrats are not becoming extremist at the rate I had feared.There is some real bipartisan movement on good policymaking at the federal level.The nation is waking up to the problem of corruption, and holding the perpetrators to account.Liberals, not leftists, are leading the anti-Trump chargeOver the past few years, I’ve watched the emergence of a leftist faction within the Democratic Party, which I’ve likened to MAGA on the right. This faction had its roots in the Bernie insurgency of 2016-2020, but it has grown beyond that. The Palestine movement both invigorated the leftists and radicalized them, shifting the locus of power in left-of-center activism away from Black activists, identitarian movements, and anti-capitalism, and toward explicitly anti-American “decolonial” ideas. As recently as this summer, I believed that a Democratic victory in the midterms would be led by this hard-left vanguard:Are the Democrats going to save us this time? Noah Smith·Aug 6Read full storyHere’s what I wrote:Democrats have spent their political capital moving to the left…[They are selecting] candidates who are so far to the left that they end up frightening and/or offending many voters, and then basically daring people to keep voting for the Republicans…When DSA-type candidates were just winning in deep blue cities, it was possible to think that they would remain a small, limited faction within the party. But Francesca Hong is going to be the Democratic nominee in a statewide race. So is Abdul El-Sayed, who, while not a member of the DSA, is closely aligned with them (especially on Israel, which he focuses on a lot)…This, increasingly, is who the Democrats are now.Well, happily, I was wrong about this. Francesca Hong was actually defeated in the Democratic primary race just a few days later in a stunning upset, showing that even partisan Democrats aren’t sold on the DSA faction. Even more importantly, the hard left didn’t end up leading the anti-Trump charge in the midterms, as I had expected. Despite the blue wave, most of the high-profile DSA-faction candidates performed significantly worse than their normie Democrat counterparts. Jeff Maurer has great data on this:I Might Be WrongHow Leftists and Moderates Did in the MidtermsThree months ago, I wrote a post “setting up the goal posts” to measure how individual candidates did in the midterms. I did that for two reasons: First, I did it to be a dick. I feel that liberals can be too polite, and we bite our tongues in response to the hate and idiocy that DSA types are trying to smuggle into the mainstream — I see a role for a t…Read more11 days ago · 307 likes · 140 comments · Jeff MaurerAnd the same voters who powered the big Democratic victories also endorsed a lot of centrist policies at the ballot box. Here’s the Washington Post:Voters in North Carolina elected a Democratic senator…giving former governor Roy Cooper an overwhelming win. At the same time, they approved three [Republican] measures…The first would add a constitutional requirement for a levy limit on property taxes…The second would cap the state income tax at 3.5 percent…The third would require photo ID for voting…In Wisconsin, Democrat David Crowley won the gubernatorial election…Those same voters approved an initiative…to ban affirmative action in state institutions…Iowa voters elected Democrats as governor and senator while amending their constitution to make it substantially harder to raise state income taxes…Ohio….went blue for Senate and governor. At the same time, two-thirds of voters backed an amendment to require photo ID for voting…Moderates and independents drove Democratic gains in all these places.Voters in several blue and purple states also approved measures to restrict women’s sports teams by biological sex.There’s also a general indefinable “vibe shift” in the air. Anecdotally, people I talk to are less ashamed to voice full-throated support for the kind of liberalism that Barack Obama typified in the early 2010s. Meanwhile, liberal influencers online are beginning to push back more strongly on leftist shouters. And in Congress, the sheer scale of the Democrats’ victory means that the DSA faction will be effectively disempowered. Because marginal victories tend to be won by moderates in purple states, the leadership in both the House and the Senate is likely to be held by moderates like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer. This is driving the DSA factionalist types apoplectic with rage:Nathan J Robinson@NathanJRobinsonI have come to the conclusion that Hakeem Jeffries is the most serious threat to the progressive agenda in the country, more so than Trump himself, and that any progressive not loudly, actively opposing Jeffries is actively betraying their movement.10:37 AM · Nov 11, 2026 · 334K Views489 Replies · 1.73K Reposts · 9.72K LikesKen Klippenstein@kenklippensteinOpposing a Washington Generals-level loser like Chuck Schumer for Senate leader is the easiest layup in politics. Any Democrat who doesn’t should be off the 2028 shortlist. Example: Jon Ossoff7:38 PM · Nov 5, 2026 · 239K Views160 Replies · 953 Reposts · 11.2K LikesKen Klippenstein@kenklippensteinChuck Schumer loves Jon Ossoff and you should ask yourself why that is7:45 PM · Nov 5, 2026 · 1.05M Views758 Replies · 1.89K Reposts · 18.4K LikesNote that the knives are already coming out for Jon Ossoff, whose potential as a 2028 presidential contender surged after his massive midterm victory. But who can leftists run against Ossoff? Enthusiasm around AOC has dimmed, and there’s no obvious replacement. If they fail to find a candidate for 2028, and if Democrats take back the White House with a normie liberal, the leftist faction faces the real possibility that the window of America’s decade of unrest will limp to a close without them. That would, of course, be good for the nation. Smart policy is starting to win (and “the groups” are starting to lose)Even moderate politicians, of course, often support unworkable or inadvisable policies. On the Democratic side, the worst problems are anti-development policies at the state and local level. “Progressive” policies have made it prohibitively difficult and/or expensive to build housing, roads, trains, power stations, and transmission lines across much of the country, freezing our built environment in the 1970s. I’ve been loudly complaining about this for years now:The Build-Nothing CountryNoah Smith·February 27, 2023Read full storyThis was a big part of my pessimism about politics. What’s the use of kicking out the Republicans, if the Democrats are just going to decide that “open space” and historic gas stations are more important than giving the middle class a place to live and power for their homes? Now there are signs that at long last, America’s leaders recognize this problem and are taking action to fix it.Continue reading this post for free, courtesy of Noah Smith.Or purchase a paid subscription.
